{{Short description|Number that has a perfect number of factors adding up to another perfect number}}
In [[number theory]], a '''sublime number''' is a [[Positive real numbers|positive]] [[integer]] which has a [[perfect number]] of positive [[Factorization|factors ]] (including itself), and whose positive factors add up to another perfect number.<ref>MathPages article, [http://www.mathpages.com/home/kmath202/kmath202.htm "Sublime Numbers"].</ref>

The number [[12 (number)|12]], for example, is a sublime number.  It has a perfect number of positive factors ([[6 (number)|6]]): 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12, and the sum of these is again a perfect number: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 12 = [[28 (number)|28]].

{{As of|July 2026}}, there are only two known sublime numbers: 12 and (2<sup>126</sup>)(2<sup>61</sup> − 1)(2<sup>31</sup> − 1)(2<sup>19</sup> − 1)(2<sup>7</sup> − 1)(2<sup>5</sup> − 1)(2<sup>3</sup> − 1)  {{OEIS|id=A081357}}.<ref>[[Clifford A. Pickover]], ''Wonders of Numbers, Adventures in Mathematics, Mind and Meaning'' New York: Oxford University Press (2003): 215</ref> The second of these has 76 decimal digits:
:6,086,555,670,238,378,989,670,371,734,243,169,622,657,830,773,351,885,970,528,324,860,512,791,691,264.
It has 8128 positive divisors, which all add up to 2<sup>126</sup>(2<sup>127</sup>-1), the 12th even perfect number (by the [[Euclid–Euler theorem]], since 2<sup>127</sup>-1 is the 12th [[Mersenne prime]]).
